analysis.one_liner: Bars debt collectors from suing over debts whose legal time limit has expired.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: after a 2011 referral to the House Financial Services Committee and its subcommittee, no hearing, markup, or vote followed before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a debt is too old to sue over — the statute of limitations has run out — debt collectors today can still threaten a lawsuit to scare people into paying. This bill would make it illegal for a collector to sue or threaten to sue on such a 'time-barred' debt. It would also require collectors to tell consumers, in plain terms, that the debt has been sold or transferred, that the collector cannot win a lawsuit over it, and that any payment they make could restart the legal clock and make the debt fully collectible again.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers being pursued over old debts, especially low-income people without lawyers who cannot tell that a collector has no legal way to win in court. They would be spared default judgments, wage garnishment, and the trap of accidentally reviving an expired debt by paying a little of it.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a debt collector from bringing or threatening legal action on a debt whose statute of limitations has expired.

Requires collectors to disclose that the debt was transferred, that the original creditor no longer holds it, that no lawsuit can be brought because the statute of limitations has run out, and that any payment may reset the statute of limitations.

analysis.who_pays: Debt buyers and collection agencies, whose business model often depends on suing on old, cheaply purchased debts or pressuring payments that legally revive them. Some legitimate creditors also might see slightly less recovery on truly aged receivables.

drawbacks.text: Collectors argue the statute of limitations alone tells consumers a lawsuit is barred, and that the required disclosures add compliance costs on every communication about an aged debt; some old debts are genuinely owed, and consumers might misunderstand the disclosures as meaning they owe nothing at all.
The bill addresses only debt collectors, not original creditors, so a creditor could still sue directly on a time-barred debt it holds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete for a vulnerable group: lawsuits and threats over expired debts are a documented way collectors extract money people do not legally owe, and a payment trap can turn an uncollectible debt into a fully enforceable one. The costs are limited to added disclosure requirements and foregone recoveries on debts the law already treats as too old to enforce. The main design gap is that it binds collectors but not original creditors.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee, then to a subcommittee, and stayed there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 24, 2011 by Rep. Steve Cohen and referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
On July 19, 2011 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and no further action was recorded for the remainder of the 112th Congress.
The bill had four cosponsors, all Democrats, and never advanced past the committee stage.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt buyers and collection agencies that profit from lawsuits and payment-pressure on expired debts are better off, since no rule restricting the practice was ever enacted; the bipartisan currents that later produced CFPB rules on time-barred debt did not run through this bill.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought to move it through the House Financial Services Committee.

for.name: Reps. Jesse Jackson Jr., Jim McDermott, Gregory Meeks, and Barbara Lee

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Republican-chaired in the 112th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never held a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: Debt collection and debt-buying industry
against.what_they_did: Had an interest in keeping suits and payment demands on expired debts available; no formal opposition appears in the congressional record, and none was needed because the bill never moved.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no formal opposition was recorded; the bill's support was entirely Democratic (one sponsor plus four Democratic cosponsors), and the Republican-controlled committee simply never acted on it.

industries.note: These firms buy old, expired debts for pennies and profit by suing consumers or pressing for payments that legally reset the clock on a debt the holder could never win in court. The bill would bar the lawsuits and force disclosures that undercut that pressure, eliminating a revenue stream built on debts the law already treats as unenforceable.

The bill does not bind original creditors, who could still sue on their own time-barred debts, but collectors' disclosures that a creditor 'no longer holds the debt' and may not sue would still make aged receivables harder to monetize through sale.
